analysis.investment_thesis: Curis Lifesciences fails both legs of the Magic Formula: earnings yield of ~5.9% (1/P.E of 16.90) is well below the 12%+ threshold, and an ROE of 0.55% signals near-zero return on capital — the hallmark of a mediocre business, not a great one. There is no Magic Formula case here.
key_strengths: High promoter holding (68%) signals skin in the game
Pharma sector can generate high ROIC if competitive moat exists
Small market cap (₹74 Cr) means institutional neglect — mispricing possible in theory
key_risks: ROE of 0.55% is essentially zero — the business destroys value on equity deployed
Earnings yield ~5.9% (1/16.9 P/E) is below Greenblatt's 12% attractiveness floor
Micro-cap pharma with no demonstrated earnings power — extremely high business quality risk
red_flags: ROE of 0.55% — catastrophically low, likely means razor-thin or near-break-even earnings
EBIT/EV (true earnings yield) likely even worse than the 5.9% implied by P/E once debt is factored in
Insufficient disclosure of EBIT, working capital, and fixed assets — Magic Formula cannot be fully computed
No evidence of sustained ROIC above cost of capital over any time period
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Magic Formula standpoint, Curis Lifesciences fails on both criteria simultaneously — the rarest and worst outcome. Implied earnings yield from P/E of 16.90 is approximately 5.9%, already below my minimum threshold of 12% EBIT/EV. The true EBIT/EV is likely lower once debt is added to enterprise value, making the valuation even less attractive. Greenblatt's framework demands you pay a bargain price — Curis offers no such margin of safety.

The return-on-capital picture is worse. ROE of 0.55% means the business earns less than 1 rupee for every 200 rupees of equity — effectively destroying shareholder value in real terms after inflation. A great business (25%+ ROIC) bought at any reasonable price is preferable to this. With no data demonstrating sustained EBIT growth, high FCF conversion, or competitive moat, Curis simply doesn't belong in a Magic Formula portfolio at any price near current levels.
